details:
**Bokanovsky's Process**
The technique at the Central London Hatchery and Conditioning Centre that makes one fertilized egg bud into as many as 96 identical embryos, mass-producing workers for the lower castes. The novel opens with a tour of the hatchery, "a squat grey building of only thirty-four stories." Podsnap's Technique, which speeds up the ripening of eggs, supplements it.

**Soma**
The state-issued drug that gives instant, hangover-free happiness and keeps the population docile. It is handed out to workers each day and used at Solidarity Services and orgies.

**John the Savage**
The son of Linda and the Director, born and raised on the Savage Reservation, who learns about the world from an old copy of The Complete Works of Shakespeare and constantly quotes it. Brought to London, he rejects its shallow pleasures, retreats to an abandoned air-lighthouse, whips himself, and hangs himself at the end. The cryptic final lines describe his dangling feet slowly turning like compass needles.

**Mustapha Mond**
The Resident World Controller for Western Europe. In a long debate with John, he defends the World State's trade of art, religion, and truth for stability, while admitting he has read Shakespeare and the Bible. John claims "the right to be unhappy." Mond also explains that the order was founded after the chemical and biological devastation of the Nine Years' War, and he exiles Bernard and Helmholtz to islands.

**Bernard Marx**
An Alpha-Plus psychologist who is unusually short and feels inadequate; rumor says alcohol was accidentally put in his blood-surrogate as an embryo. The Director threatens to transfer him to Iceland. He brings John and Linda back from the reservation, enjoys brief celebrity, and is finally exiled to an island.

**Linda, Pope, and the Malpais reservation**
Linda, a Beta, became pregnant with the Director's child (she knew him as "Tomakin") and was left behind at the Malpais reservation in New Mexico. There she was shunned by the villagers and had an affair with Pope, who brought her mescal; a jealous young John tried to stab him. Back in London she drowns herself in soma and dies at a hospital where children are being "death-conditioned," mistaking John for Pope.

**The Director called "my father"**
The Director of Hatcheries and Conditioning (Thomas) plans to humiliate Bernard publicly. Bernard instead brings in Linda and John, who falls to his knees and calls the Director "my father." The scandalous word causes the Director to resign in disgrace.

**Helmholtz Watson and the Falkland Islands**
A brilliant Alpha lecturer at the College of Emotional Engineering who gets in trouble for reading his students a heretical poem about solitude. He becomes John's friend. After the riot, Mond lets him choose a place of exile, and he picks the Falkland Islands for its bad climate, hoping it will improve his writing.

**Lenina Crowne and "impudent strumpet"**
A pretty, popular Beta hatchery worker who visits the reservation with Bernard and is attracted to John. When she undresses to seduce him, he rages at her as an "impudent strumpet" (quoting Othello) and drives her off. She later appears at the lighthouse, where he whips her, which leads to a soma-fueled orgy.

**Hypnopaedia**
Sleep-teaching used to condition values through endlessly repeated phrases, such as "everyone belongs to everyone else," "ending is better than mending," and "civilization is sterilization." In Neo-Pavlovian conditioning, Delta babies are given electric shocks when they reach for books and flowers so they will hate reading and nature.

**Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, Epsilon**
The five castes of the World State, named for Greek letters, from the intelligent Alphas down to the semi-moronic Epsilons. Each is engineered and conditioned for its place in society.

**Three Weeks in a Helicopter and the "feelies"**
The "feelies" are films that let audiences feel what is on screen, accompanied by a scent organ and synthetic music. John is taken to Three Weeks in a Helicopter, condemns it as "base" and "ignoble," and is reminded of Linda and Pope.

**Ford, the sign of the T, and 632 A.F.**
Henry Ford is worshiped as a messianic figure ("Our Ford"), and people make the sign of the T across their stomachs. Years are counted "After Ford," and the novel is set in 632 A.F. Bernard attends a Solidarity Service ending in the chant "Orgy-porgy."

**The Delta riot at the hospital**
After Linda's death, John throws the Deltas' soma ration out a window and urges them to be free, starting a riot. Police calm the crowd with soma vapor and a Synthetic Music Box, and John, Bernard, and Helmholtz are arrested and brought before Mond.

**Title from The Tempest**
The title comes from Miranda's line in Shakespeare's The Tempest, "O brave new world, that has such people in't!", which John quotes. Huxley later wrote the essay collection Brave New World Revisited (1958), including the essay "Quantity, Quality, Morality."
